title: Hybrid token-split scheduler with kernel-hinting for latency-fairness tradeoffs
creator: Anya Patel
description:
Problem: Our current prefill/decode arbitration groups requests mostly by arrival window and sequence-length heuristics, which can cause poor latency for short interactive queries when mixed with long streaming decodes. It also leaves kernel selection decisions coupled tightly to the final batch composition, preventing early routing to low-latency kernel paths.

Proposal: Implement a hybrid token-split scheduler that: 1) emits a lightweight per-request kernel-hint at prefill time (low-latency vs throughput-optimized) based on prompt template, requested max tokens, and historical tail behavior; 2) performs an early micro-split of prefill and decode phases into 'fast-path' and 'bulk-path' queues using proportional fairness tokens; 3) keeps kernel-hint attached through batching and informs the runtime kernel selector prior to kernel probe; 4) supports opportunistic hedging: if fast-path queue backs up beyond a latency budget, allow a small fraction of fast-path requests to be promoted to hedged GPU slots to avoid head-of-line blocking.

Why this is different: Existing approaches we have explored (phase-slicing, temporal windowing) focus on window/phase partitioning alone. This design explicitly separates kernel-selection signalling from final batch packing and uses it as a first-class input to scheduling decisions. By doing so, the runtime can prefer latency-optimized kernels for short interactions without sacrificing bulk throughput for long decodes.

High-level goals: Reduce p99 latency for short (<128 tokens) interactive requests by 20-30% in mixed workloads while keeping aggregate GPU utilization loss under 5% and reducing long-request tail regressions.

Key design details: - Kernel-hint generation: lightweight heuristic model (rule-based with optional small classifier) that tags requests with one of [latency, balanced, throughput]. Source signals: client-requested max_tokens, model_id, prompt pattern fingerprint, recent session history. - Micro-split policy: use a token-credit allocator that assigns fairness credits per customer and per priority tier; fast-path gets reserved token credits sized by historical short-request ratio per customer. - Batch formation: batches prefer homogeneous kernel-hint to avoid kernel-switching overhead; small mixed batches allowed with a fast-path reservation fraction. - Hedging: if fast-path queue delay > budget (configurable by SLA tier), spawn hedged micro-batch on an opportunistic slot or route to lower-latency model variant. - Telemetry & observability: emit kernel-hint and queue-duration tags on traces, per-model kernel-switch counts, and hedged-run rates.

Tradeoffs and risks: - Additional metadata on requests increases control-plane and trace cardinality; mitigate by sampling and compact hint encoding. - Homogeneous batches by kernel-hint can reduce batch sizes (throughput loss); we mitigate with fractional coalescing windows and by allowing throughput-labeled requests to absorb slack. - Hedging increases GPU load; cap hedging rate by SLA and backpressure signals. - Heuristic misclassification could route medium-length requests to low-latency kernels leading to regressions; plan to iterate with small classifier and offline replays.

Implementation plan (phases): 1) Simulation & replay: extend trace replayer to synthesize kernel-hint signals and evaluate latency/throughput tradeoffs offline. 2) Instrumentation: add kernel-hint tagging to prefill path and minimal trace tags. 3) Scheduler prototype: implement micro-split allocator + hint-aware batcher on dev cluster; run A/B against synthetic mixed workload. 4) Canary rollout: start with non-critical models and internal customers, monitor p50/p95/p99, GPU utilization, and kernel-switch counters. 5) Gradual scale-up and policy tuning.

Acceptance criteria (see field for full list): see acceptance_criteria below.
acceptance_criteria: Simulated replay shows >=20% reduction in p99 for <128-token requests on mixed traces with <5% GPU utilization regression
Kernel-hint telemetry available in traces and dashboard; kernel-switch metric added to runtime metrics
Scheduler prototype deployed to dev cluster and passes synthetic load tests (no SLA regressions for existing customers)
Canary rollout shows hedging does not exceed configured cap and reduces fast-path queue time under latency budget
Runbook updated with knob descriptions, throttles, and rollback steps
